analysis.one_liner: Bans cruise ships from dumping untreated sewage and wastewater in U.S. waters and requires inspections and penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Sen. Durbin with 5 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Cruise ships could no longer dump untreated sewage, graywater from sinks and showers, or oily bilge water into U.S. waters [S3]. Treated discharges would have to meet federal limits, ships would face annual unannounced inspections, and each line would pay a fee of up to $10 per passenger to fund enforcement [S3]. Crew members who reported violations would be protected from being fired [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: People who swim, fish, and live along U.S. coasts and in the Great Lakes, and the coastal tourism economies that depend on clean water. The bill's own findings describe cruise ship sewage as harming coral reefs and raising pathogen levels in the water, and state that existing law did not adequately monitor or enforce cruise discharges [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibited cruise vessels entering U.S. ports from discharging sewage, graywater, or bilge water into U.S. waters, with narrow exceptions only when treated discharges met federal effluent limits [S2].

Required the Coast Guard and EPA to set enforceable effluent limits for sewage and graywater, including caps on fecal coliform and chlorine, and to run an inspection, sampling, and testing program with at least one unannounced inspection of each vessel per year [S3].

Gave citizens and states the right to sue violators and to sue federal agencies that failed to enforce, and offered rewards of up to half of collected penalties to people whose tips led to enforcement [S3].
Protected ship employees from being fired for reporting violations or testifying in enforcement proceedings [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The cruise industry, which would bear the cost of treatment systems, inspections, discharge logging, and a fee of up to $10 per paying passenger to fund the enforcement program [S3]. Those costs would likely be passed along to cruise passengers in ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Cruise operators would have faced substantial compliance costs — advanced treatment equipment, unannounced inspections, discharge logbooks and blueprints, and a per-passenger fee of up to $10 that would likely be added to ticket prices [S3].
The bill carved out a long exemption for Alaskan cruise vessels: ships already certified with advanced treatment systems would be subject to most of the Act only 15 years after enactment [S3].

Setting up a national inspection, sampling, and certification program for a foreign-flagged fleet would have been a significant enforcement undertaking for the Coast Guard, funded partly by the new fees and appropriations for fiscal years 2006 through 2010 [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — protecting coastal waters, coral reefs, and public health from cruise ship waste that existing law did not adequately control — was broad and enduring, while the costs fell on one industry and, in small part, on cruise ticket prices. The 15-year delay for Alaskan vessels that already had advanced treatment systems, and the reliance on still-to-be-written federal limits, softened the bill's immediate reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2005 and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Clean Cruise Ship Act of 2005 on April 14, 2005, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral: no hearing, no committee markup, no vote in either chamber through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cruise operators came out ahead: without the bill, they kept operating under the pre-existing rules the bill's findings called inadequate for monitoring and enforcing cruise discharges, and avoided treatment requirements, inspections, and per-passenger fees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cruise operators who avoided new discharge rules

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

for.name: 5 Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 2005 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Cruise industry
against.role: Major shipping and tourism industry (largely foreign-flagged operators)
against.what_they_did: The industry publicly resisted federal discharge limits and mandatory inspection programs for cruise ships during this period, favoring voluntary and state-by-state approaches.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters — the sponsor and five cosponsors — were Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote that would show Republican positions.

industries.note: The bill would have banned dumping untreated sewage, graywater, and oily bilge water, imposed effluent limits and annual unannounced inspections, and charged up to $10 per passenger for enforcement. Its costs would fall on an industry whose discharge practices the bill's findings said existing law failed to adequately monitor [S3].
Cleaner coastal waters and protected coral reefs support beaches, fishing, and ocean tourism. The bill cited cruise sewage as killing coral and raising pathogens in coastal waters [S3].

industries.industry: Marine wastewater treatment and monitoring technology makers
industries.note: The bill funded a pilot program to develop and commercialize real-time discharge monitoring technology, with selected industry partners contributing at least 20 percent of project costs [S3].
